title: Terminating or Repeating? Decoding Decimal Expansions 🔮
hook: Why does 1/4 = 0.25 (stops after 2 digits) but 1/3 = 0.333... (goes on forever)? It's not random — the prime factors of the denominator tell you everything! It's like a secret code hidden in every fraction.
explanation:
For a rational number p/q (in lowest terms):
If denominator q is...Decimal expansion is...Examples
Only 2s and 5s
(q = 2ⁿ × 5ᵐ)		Terminating1/8 = 1/2³ = 0.125
7/40 = 7/(2³×5) = 0.175
Has other prime factorsNon-terminating repeating1/3 = 0.333...
1/7 = 0.142857142857...
THE RULE
Terminating ⟺ q = 2ⁿ × 5ᵐ (only factors of 2 and 5)
Why does this work? To get a terminating decimal, we need to convert p/q into p'/10ⁿ form. Since 10 = 2 × 5, we can only do this if q has no prime factors other than 2 and 5.
💡 Tip: Quick check: just look at the denominator's prime factors. If you see anything other than 2 or 5, it's repeating!

try_this.question: Without actual division, determine whether 29/343 has a terminating or non-terminating repeating decimal expansion.
try_this.hint: Find the prime factorization of 343. Is it made up of only 2s and 5s?
try_this.answer: 343 = 7³. Since the denominator has a prime factor 7 (which is neither 2 nor 5), the decimal expansion of 29/343 is non-terminating repeating.

fun_fact: The decimal expansion of 1/7 = 0.142857142857... has a repeating block of 6 digits. And those 6 digits (142857) form a 'cyclic number' — multiply it by 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, or 6 and you get the same digits in a different order! 142857 × 2 = 285714, × 3 = 428571! 🤯
